lessons.title: What storage remembers: the BTK floppy disk (2005)

blocks.md:
The course *incident-response-forensics* taught you to acquire a disk image, hash it and keep custody. This course is about what you do next: reading the image. **Disk and file system forensics** means recovering and interpreting what storage holds, including what its owner thinks is gone. **Mobile forensics** applies the same ideas to phones, where encryption changes the rules.

A tiny example first. You delete a file called `notes.doc`. Your computer does not scrub its bytes; it marks the space as free and forgets the name. Until something new is written over that space, the old bytes, and often the old name, are still on the disk. That single fact caught a serial killer.

**The case.** A serial killer in Wichita, Kansas, who used the name BTK, had been sending messages to police. Before mailing a disk, the killer asked police whether a floppy disk could be traced: *"Can I communicate with Floppy and not be traced to a computer. Be honest."* ([Oxygen](https://www.oxygen.com/snapped/crime-time/floppy-disk-exposed-dennis-rader-btk-killer)).

A lilac floppy disk arrived at a Wichita TV station in a mailing on 16 February 2005 ([Deseret News](https://www.deseret.com/2005/3/2/19879898/disk-may-have-led-to-btk-arrest/)). Its visible file held instructions for detectives. Randy Stone, a Wichita police officer skilled with computers, examined it: forensic software recovered **deleted** files and hidden data showing that the disk had been used on a computer at Christ Lutheran Church by a user named "Dennis". The church's website listed Dennis Rader as president of the congregation, and police arrested Rader on 25 February 2005 ([Oxygen](https://www.oxygen.com/snapped/crime-time/floppy-disk-exposed-dennis-rader-btk-killer)).

The church's pastor later said Rader had brought a floppy disk to the church in January, saying it held a council meeting agenda that needed printing ([Lawrence Journal-World](https://www2.ljworld.com/news/2005/mar/04/computer_disk_dna/)).

blocks.title: Where the BTK evidence sat, layer by layer

scenes.caption: Every investigation reads storage in layers. The disk is just numbered blocks; meaning appears only as you climb.
The visible layer: the file system listed the file BTK meant to send. A naive look stops here.
Deletion freed the earlier files' directory entries and space, but their bytes stayed in blocks on the disk. Forensic software recovered them.
The recovered data recorded where and by whom the disk had been used: a computer at Christ Lutheran Church, user "Dennis". A name and a place, from files the sender believed were gone.

blocks.prompt: The disk's directory listed only the message file. Before reading on: where could a second, deleted document have come from, given that Rader had used this disk on another computer?
blocks.reveal:
The disk had been used before. Rader had brought a floppy to the church in January to print a council agenda, and data deleted from the disk pointed to a church computer and a user "Dennis". Deleting freed the space but did not erase the bytes, and nothing later overwrote them. The disk carried its own history.

Note what the evidence did **not** do: it named an account ("Dennis") and a place, not a person at a keyboard. Reporting at the time says DNA, obtained from a tissue sample in the medical records of Rader's daughter, then linked Rader to the killings ([Lawrence Journal-World](https://www2.ljworld.com/news/2005/mar/04/computer_disk_dna/)).

blocks.md:
**The method behind every lesson.** NIST SP 800-86 (a 2006 guide from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology on forensics in incident response) splits the work into four phases:

1. **Collection**: identifying, labelling, recording and acquiring data while preserving its integrity. You did this in the prereq.
2. **Examination**: processing the collected data with automated and manual methods and extracting what matters. Most of this course: file systems, deleted files, Windows artefacts, phones.
3. **Analysis**: deriving useful information from the examination results, with legally justifiable methods, to answer the questions that started the work.
4. **Reporting**: presenting results, including how tools were chosen and what other explanations were considered. The last lessons.

The course goes down the stack first (disks, partitions, FAT, NTFS, ext4, APFS, carving), then up into Windows user activity, then phones, then the people problems: encryption at arrest, anti-forensics, tool trust and court.
Deleting a file usually removes the *pointer* to the data, not the data. Recovery works until the space is reused. Everything in the first half of this course is a variation on that sentence.

blocks.question: Why could examiners read a document that had been deleted from the BTK floppy?
options: Floppy disks keep a hidden backup copy of every file
Forensic software can reverse any overwrite by reading residual magnetism
Deletion marked the space as free but left the file's bytes in place, and nothing had overwritten them yet
The deleted file was still listed as live in the directory
blocks.explain: Deletion freed the entry and the space; the content stayed until reused. There is no hidden backup on a floppy, and overwritten data is not recoverable with standard tools. The directory listed only the message file, so the earlier files were not live.

blocks.question: An examiner has recovered the deleted files and now asks: does data showing use by "Dennis" on a church computer identify the sender, and how strongly? Which NIST SP 800-86 phase is this?
options: Analysis
Collection
Examination
Reporting
blocks.explain: Recovering the files and their metadata was examination. Weighing what the facts mean for the question being asked is analysis. Reporting comes after, when the conclusion and its limits are written down.

lessons.title: From sectors to partitions to image files

blocks.md:
Storage hardware presents a **block device**: a long row of fixed-size blocks, usually 512 or 4096 bytes each, that can be read or written by number. The block device has no idea what a file is ([CyBOK Forensics](https://www.cybok.org/media/downloads/Forensics_v1.0.1.pdf), the forensics knowledge area of the UK-funded Cyber Security Body of Knowledge). A **sector** is the old name for a magnetic disk's transfer unit; **LBA** (logical block addressing) simply numbers blocks from 0. Imaging, which you learned in the prereq, copies this row of blocks, so everything else must be found inside it.

Tiny example: a 9 MiB lab disk we built for this course (`disk.img`, made in our scratch folder with a script) holds 18,432 sectors of 512 bytes. Sector 0 is special.

**MBR** (master boot record, the first sector of a disk) holds a partition table. Per the UEFI specification ([UEFI 2.10, chapter 5](https://uefi.org/specs/UEFI/2.10/05_GUID_Partition_Table_Format.html)): four 16-byte partition records start at byte 446, and bytes 510 and 511 hold the signature 0x55 0xAA. In each record, byte 4 is the partition type, bytes 8 to 11 the starting LBA and bytes 12 to 15 the size in sectors, both little-endian (least significant byte first).

**GPT** (GUID Partition Table; a GUID is a globally unique identifier) is the modern scheme. Its header sits at LBA 1 and starts with the ASCII string `EFI PART`. LBA 0 then holds a *protective MBR* with a single record of type 0xEE covering the whole disk, so old tools see the disk as full rather than empty.

blocks.title: Reading one MBR partition record (lab disk, bytes 446 to 461)

scenes.caption: The 16 raw bytes of the first partition record, exactly as they sit on our lab disk.
Byte 4 is the partition type. We set 0x06 when building the image; the boot sector inside will tell us the real file system.
Bytes 8 to 11, little-endian: 00 08 00 00 reads as 0x00000800 = 2048. The partition starts at sector 2048, byte 2048 x 512 = 1,048,576.
Bytes 12 to 15: 00 40 00 00 is 0x4000 = 16,384 sectors, which is 8 MiB. Sectors 1 to 2047 belong to no partition: check them too.

blocks.code:
import struct, sys
with open(sys.argv[1], 'rb') as f:
    lba0 = f.read(512)                        # sector 0 = the MBR
print('signature ok' if lba0[510:512] == b'\x55\xaa' else 'no MBR signature')
for i in range(4):                            # four 16-byte partition records
    rec = lba0[446 + 16*i : 446 + 16*(i+1)]
    ptype = rec[4]
    start, count = struct.unpack_from('<II', rec, 8)
    if ptype == 0:
        continue                              # empty slot
    print(f'partition {i}: type 0x{ptype:02x}, start LBA {start} '
          f'(byte {start*512}), {count} sectors = {count*512 // 2**20} MiB')
    if ptype == 0xEE:
        print('  protective MBR: read the GPT header at LBA 1 ("EFI PART")')
blocks.caption: mbr.py: list the partitions in an MBR. Read-only; run it on an image, never on a live evidence drive.

blocks.code:
$ python mbr.py disk.img
signature ok
partition 0: type 0x06, start LBA 2048 (byte 1048576), 16384 sectors = 8 MiB
blocks.caption: Real output on our lab disk.

blocks.md: Do not stop at the partitions. NIST SP 800-86 counts *free space* (areas not allocated to any partition, including whole deleted volumes) as a place where data may remain. Our lab disk already has 2,047 sectors before the first partition that no file system owns.

blocks.question: A partition record says the partition starts at LBA 2048 and the disk uses 512-byte sectors. At what byte offset in the image does the partition's boot sector begin?
blocks.explain: Byte offset = LBA x sector size = 2048 x 512 = 1,048,576. 2,048 forgets the multiplication, 524,288 uses 256-byte sectors, and 2,097,152 uses 1024-byte sectors.

blocks.question: An MBR shows exactly one partition, type 0xEE, covering the whole disk. What should your tool do next?
options: Report a single unformatted partition
Read the GPT header at LBA 1 and its partition entries; the MBR is only a protective placeholder
Treat the disk as wiped, since 0xEE marks erased space
Search for 0x55 0xAA signatures to find hidden MBRs
blocks.explain: Type 0xEE is the GPT protective MBR. The real partition table is the GPT starting at LBA 1 (signature EFI PART). It does not mean unformatted or wiped.

lessons.title: What deleting a file really does: a FAT walk-through

blocks.md:
Every file system solves the same four problems: **names** (which file is called what, in which folder), **metadata** (size, times, attributes), **allocation** (which blocks are in use) and **content**. Deletion changes some of these and not others, and the difference is where evidence lives.

FAT is the simplest real example. It is named after its **File Allocation Table**: an array with one entry per *cluster* (the allocation unit, a fixed group of sectors). Each entry holds the number of the file's next cluster, so a file is a chain. Microsoft's on-disk description ([FAT: General Overview of On-Disk Format](https://www.cs.miami.edu/home/burt/learning/Csc521.071/docs/FatFormat.pdf)) defines: a free cluster has entry value 0; on FAT16 a value of 0xFFF8 or more marks the end of a chain.

A FAT **directory entry** is 32 bytes. The ones we need: bytes 0 to 10 hold the 8.3 name (eight characters, then a three-character extension), byte 11 the attributes, bytes 26 and 27 the first cluster and bytes 28 to 31 the size. The specification says that if the first byte of the name is 0xE5, *the directory entry is free*; 0x00 means free and no more entries follow.

So a FAT driver typically deletes a file by writing 0xE5 over the name's first byte and setting the file's chain entries to 0. The size, the first cluster and the content clusters are left as they were.

Our lab: we made an 8 MiB FAT16 volume (a 16-bit FAT) with the open-source pyfatfs library, wrote `NOTES.TXT` and `PHOTO.JPG` (a 1,174-byte JPEG we generated), then deleted `PHOTO.JPG` exactly as the specification describes.

blocks.title: Deleting PHOTO.JPG on our FAT16 lab volume

scenes.caption: Before: the directory entry spells PHOTO JPG, starts at cluster 3 and is 0x496 = 1,174 bytes. FAT[3] points to cluster 4; FAT[4] = FFFF ends the chain.
Delete: the first name byte becomes E5 (entry free) and FAT[3] and FAT[4] become 0000 (clusters free). Nothing else in the entry changes.
What survives: start cluster 3 and size 1,174 are intact. Read 1,174 bytes from cluster 3 onward and you have the file, if the clusters were contiguous and not reused.

blocks.code:
import struct, hashlib, sys
disk = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
ptype, lba, nsec = struct.unpack_from('<4xB3xII', disk, 446)   # first MBR record
print(f'MBR: type 0x{ptype:02x}, starts at LBA {lba}, {nsec} sectors')
v = disk[lba*512:]                                             # the FAT volume
bps, spc, rsv, nfats, nroot = struct.unpack_from('<HBHBH', v, 11)
spf = struct.unpack_from('<H', v, 22)[0]
serial = struct.unpack_from('<I', v, 39)[0]                     # BS_VolID
print(f'FAT16: {bps*spc}-byte clusters, volume serial {serial>>16:04X}-{serial&0xFFFF:04X}')
fat, root = rsv*bps, (rsv + nfats*spf)*bps
data = root + nroot*32
for i in range(0, nroot*32, 32):
    e = v[root+i:root+i+32]
    if e[0] == 0x00: break                  # no more entries
    if e[11] & 0x08: continue               # volume label or long-name piece
    name = (e[0:8].rstrip() + b'.' + e[8:11]).decode('latin-1')
    clus, size = struct.unpack_from('<HI', e, 26)
    nxt = struct.unpack_from('<H', v, fat + 2*clus)[0]
    state = 'DELETED' if e[0] == 0xE5 else 'live   '
    if e[0] == 0xE5: name = '?' + name[1:]   # first letter is gone
    print(f'{state} {name:12} cluster {clus}  {size:5} bytes  FAT[{clus}]=0x{nxt:04X}')
    if e[0] == 0xE5:                        # data may still be there
        off = data + (clus-2)*bps*spc
        blob = v[off:off+size]
        print(f'        first bytes {blob[:4].hex()}  sha256 {hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest()[:16]}')

blocks.code:
$ python fat_list.py disk.img
MBR: type 0x06, starts at LBA 2048, 16384 sectors
FAT16: 1024-byte clusters, volume serial 1234-ABCD
live    NOTES.TXT    cluster 2     25 bytes  FAT[2]=0xFFFF
DELETED ?HOTO.JPG    cluster 3   1174 bytes  FAT[3]=0x0000
        first bytes ffd8ffe0  sha256 fb067d78afd6c66a
$ shasum -a 256 photo.jpg | cut -c1-16   # the original we wrote
fb067d78afd6c66a
blocks.caption: Real output. The recovered bytes hash to the same SHA-256 as the original JPEG, so the recovery is exact. The first letter of the name is gone: 0xE5 overwrote it.

blocks.md:
**Why this works, and when it fails.**

- The recovery assumed the file's clusters were *contiguous* (3, then 4). The chain that would tell us otherwise was zeroed. A fragmented file recovered this way is right for the first fragment and garbage after it.
- If a new file has since been allocated cluster 3, you recover the new file's bytes under the old name.
- **Slack space** is the unused tail of the last cluster. NIST SP 800-86's example: with 32 KB clusters a 7 KB file leaves 25 KB of slack, which may hold remnants of older files. In our image `NOTES.TXT` is 25 bytes in a 1,024-byte cluster, leaving 999 bytes of slack.

The volume serial number printed above (1234-ABCD, from the boot sector field `BS_VolID`) matters later: Windows records it when files on this volume are opened.

Floppy disks use FAT: Microsoft has described it as the only file system Windows supports on floppies ([FAT32 File System](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/aa364047%28v=vs.85%29)). So the BTK disk was almost certainly FAT-formatted, and its deleted files survived for the reason shown above: nothing had reused their space yet.

blocks.question: A deleted FAT file's entry says first cluster 3, size 5,000 bytes, 1,024-byte clusters. Unknown to you, the file was stored in clusters 3, 4, 9, 10 and 11. You recover 5,000 bytes from cluster 3 onward. What do you get?
options: The exact file, because FAT keeps a backup chain
The first 2,048 bytes correct, then whatever sits in clusters 5 to 7
Nothing, because a deleted entry has no first cluster
The exact file, because FAT never fragments files
blocks.explain: Clusters 3 and 4 are right (2,048 bytes). Deletion zeroed the chain, so the jump to 9 is lost and you read clusters 5, 6, 7 instead. The entry keeps the first cluster; there is no backup chain; and FAT files can fragment.

blocks.question: After deletion, which piece of the PHOTO.JPG directory entry is gone for good?
options: The first character of its name
Its size
Its first cluster number
Its extension
blocks.explain: Deletion overwrote only the name's first byte with 0xE5. Size, first cluster and extension remain, which is why tools show deleted names as ?HOTO.JPG or _HOTO.JPG.

lessons.title: NTFS and the master file table, record by record

blocks.md:
NTFS is the primary file system of Windows versions based on Windows NT. Its centre is the **MFT** (master file table). Per Microsoft ([Master File Table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/master-file-table)), every file, including the MFT itself, has at least one MFT entry; everything about a file is stored in entries or in space they describe; and a deleted file's entry is *marked as free and may be reused*.

Concretely, each MFT entry is a 1,024-byte record on typical volumes (the boot sector states the size) starting with the ASCII signature `FILE`. The first records are the file system's own metadata files ([libfsntfs notes](https://github.com/libyal/libfsntfs/blob/main/documentation/New%20Technologies%20File%20System%20%28NTFS%29.asciidoc)): 0 `$MFT`, 1 `$MFTMirr` (a backup of the first four entries), 2 `$LogFile` (metadata transaction journal), 5 the root directory, 6 `$Bitmap` (which clusters are allocated), 11 `$Extend` (a folder of newer metadata files, including the change journal of lesson 6).

Inside a record ([FILE_RECORD_SEGMENT_HEADER](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/devnotes/file-record-segment-header)):

- **Fixups.** Before writing, NTFS saves the last two bytes of each 512-byte stride in an *update sequence array* and overwrites them with a sequence number. If a stride does not end with that number on read, the write was torn. Parsers restore the saved bytes first.
- **Flags.** 0x0001 means in use; 0x0002 means it has a file name index (a directory).
- **Sequence number.** Incremented each time the record is freed. A *file reference* is the 48-bit record number plus this 16-bit sequence, so a stale reference to a reused record can be spotted.
- **Attributes** follow, each with a type code ([ATTRIBUTE_RECORD_HEADER](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/devnotes/attribute-record-header)): 0x10 `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`, 0x30 `$FILE_NAME`, 0x80 `$DATA`, 0x90 and 0xA0 for directory indexes. A list ends with 0xFFFFFFFF. *Resident* attributes keep their value inside the record; *non-resident* ones store a list of runs (cluster ranges) elsewhere.

blocks.title: Walking MFT record 41 (File.txt) in a public test image

scenes.caption: Record 41 begins with FILE. The header says: fixup array at byte 48 with 3 entries, sequence number 1, first attribute at byte 56, flags 1 (in use).
Fixups: the last 2 bytes of each 512-byte half read 0x0008, the update sequence number. The real values (here 0000) are copied back from the array before parsing.
Attribute 1 at byte 56: type 0x10, `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`, 96 bytes, resident. Its first four 8-byte values are the SI timestamps.
Attribute 2 at byte 152: type 0x30, `$FILE_NAME`: parent folder reference, four more timestamps, the name File.txt.
Then 0x40 (`$OBJECT_ID`, an identifier used for link tracking) and 0x80 (`$DATA`). This data attribute is resident: the file's text lives inside the record itself.
0xFFFFFFFF at byte 344 ends the list. Everything about File.txt fit in 344 bytes of one record.

blocks.code:
import struct, sys
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
img = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
bps, spc = struct.unpack_from('<HB', img, 11)            # NTFS boot sector
mft = struct.unpack_from('<Q', img, 48)[0] * bps * spc   # where $MFT starts

def ft(v):  # FILETIME: 100 ns ticks since 1601 UTC
    t = datetime(1601, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc) + timedelta(microseconds=v // 10)
    return f'{t:%y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}.{v % 10**7:07d}'

def record(n):
    r = bytearray(img[mft + n*1024 : mft + (n+1)*1024])
    assert r[:4] == b'FILE'
    uo, un = struct.unpack_from('<HH', r, 4)             # update sequence array
    for k in range(1, un):                               # undo the fixups
        r[k*512-2 : k*512] = r[uo + 2*k : uo + 2*k + 2]
    return r

for n in map(int, sys.argv[2:]):
    r = record(n)
    print(f'record {n}:', 'in use' if r[22] & 1 else 'FREE')
    a = struct.unpack_from('<H', r, 20)[0]               # first attribute
    while (t := struct.unpack_from('<I', r, a)[0]) != 0xFFFFFFFF:
        val = a + struct.unpack_from('<H', r, a+20)[0]   # resident value
        if t == 0x10:
            c, m = struct.unpack_from('<QQ', r, val)
            print(f'  $SI born {ft(c)}  modified {ft(m)}')
        elif t == 0x30:
            c, m = struct.unpack_from('<QQ', r, val+8)
            name = r[val+66 : val+66+2*r[val+64]].decode('utf-16-le')
            print(f'  $FN born {ft(c)}  modified {ft(m)}  {name}')
        elif t == 0x80:
            print('  $DATA', 'non-resident' if r[a+8] else 'resident')
        a += struct.unpack_from('<I', r, a+4)[0]
blocks.caption: mft_record.py: a minimal MFT record parser (fixups, flags, SI, FN and data attributes). Our test image is ntfs.bin, a 10 MB NTFS volume published as test data by the open-source dissect.ntfs project of Fox-IT (a security company that is part of NCC Group).

$ python mft_record.py ntfs.bin 41 44
record 41: in use
  $SI born 22-05-12 23:17:23.1413977  modified 22-05-12 23:17:34.9131977
  $FN born 22-05-12 23:17:23.1413977  modified 22-05-12 23:17:23.1413977  File.txt
  $DATA resident
record 44: in use
  $SI born 22-05-12 23:18:30.5897415  modified 22-05-12 23:19:04.9517170
  $FN born 22-05-12 23:18:30.5897415  modified 22-05-12 23:18:30.5897415  Large.txt
  $DATA non-resident
blocks.caption: Real output. Times are UTC, to 100-nanosecond resolution. Limit: the parser assumes `$MFT` is one contiguous run. Here it has three fragments, so only records 0 to 939 are reachable; real tools follow record 0's data runs (lesson 16).

blocks.md:
**Reading the output.** In both files the SI modified time moved after creation when content was written, while the FN times still equal the creation time. Across all 2,292 records in this image that have a file name attribute, the FN modified time equals the FN creation time, and in 220 of them SI modified is later. The two attribute sets are maintained differently, which the next lesson uses.

`Large.txt` has a non-resident data attribute: its record holds only the runs, and the content is in clusters elsewhere.

**Deleted files on NTFS.** Deleting clears the in-use flag, frees the clusters in `$Bitmap` and removes the name from the parent folder's index, but the record itself stays until it is reused. Tools such as MFTECmd (one of Eric Zimmerman's free DFIR parsers, for `$MFT`, `$J`, `$LogFile` and more; [list](https://ericzimmerman.github.io/)) report these records with in-use false, often with full names, times and, for small files, their resident content.

A free MFT record with a resident `$DATA` still contains the old file's bytes. A large file's record holds only runs, and those clusters may already belong to someone else. Always check whether the clusters a deleted record points to are now allocated before trusting the content.

blocks.question: Your parser reads an MFT record without applying fixups. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: fixups only matter for directories
The FILE signature is missing, so the record is skipped
Two bytes at the end of each 512-byte stride are wrong, which can corrupt any attribute that crosses a stride boundary
All timestamps are shifted by 100 nanoseconds
blocks.explain: The stride ends hold the update sequence number, not the real data. Attributes spanning byte 510 to 511 or 1022 to 1023 read wrong values. Fixups apply to all records, the signature is at the start and unaffected, and timestamps are not shifted.

blocks.question: Record 812 is marked free and its sequence number is 4. An entry in the NTFS change journal (lesson 6) refers to file reference 812 with sequence 3. What does that tell you?
options: The journal entry describes the same file that the record holds now
The journal is corrupt, because sequence numbers never change
Record 812 is a directory
The journal entry describes an earlier file that used record 812 before it was freed
blocks.explain: The sequence number increments each time a record is freed. Sequence 3 in the reference versus 4 in the record means the record has been freed since; the reference points to an older occupant.

lessons.title: Eight NTFS timestamps, and how timestomping gets caught

blocks.md:
Each NTFS file carries two sets of four times: **created, modified, MFT-entry modified, accessed**. One set sits in `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` (SI), one in `$FILE_NAME` (FN). Each is a FILETIME: 100-nanosecond ticks since 1 January 1601 UTC. Forensic tools label the four as MACB (modified, accessed, changed, born), as in the prereq's super timelines.

Two cautions about the accessed time: Windows can defer writing last-access updates to disk by up to one hour, and the update can be turned off entirely (`fsutil behavior` setting `disablelastaccess`; [Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/fsutil-behavior)). Treat access times as weak evidence.

**Timestomping** (MITRE ATT&CK T1070.006, under the Stealth tactic) is altering file times to hide new files or changes. ATT&CK's description ([T1070.006](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1070/006/)) explains why the two sets matter:

- SI times are what users and Explorer see; FN times are maintained by the kernel.
- Changing SI times is common because ordinary programs can do it through API calls such as `SetFileTime` (which exists for legitimate uses: installers and archive tools restore original times).
- Changing FN times typically requires kernel-level access, or moving or renaming the file.
- Some intruders try to change both ("double timestomping") precisely to defeat SI versus FN comparison.

So the comparison is a lead, not a verdict. Strong cases stack several independent signals.

blocks.title: Four witnesses to one file's birth (days since 1 March 2019)

scenes.caption: The SI creation time, what Explorer shows: 1 March 2019, 09:00:00.0000000. Plausible on its own.
The FN creation time of the same record: 12 May 2022, about 1,168.6 days later. A file cannot be born twice; one of these is wrong.
Independent witness: the change journal (next lesson) would hold a BASIC_INFO_CHANGE record, which Microsoft defines as a change to attributes or time stamps, at the moment of alteration.
Another: endpoint telemetry of the process that called SetFileTime. Several sources agreeing on 2022 outweigh one attribute claiming 2019. (Illustrative positions.)

blocks.code:
import struct, sys
img = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
bps, spc = struct.unpack_from('<HB', img, 11)
mft = struct.unpack_from('<Q', img, 48)[0] * bps * spc
nrec = int(sys.argv[2])

def times(n):
    r = bytearray(img[mft + n*1024 : mft + (n+1)*1024])
    if r[:4] != b'FILE': return None
    uo, un = struct.unpack_from('<HH', r, 4)
    for k in range(1, un): r[k*512-2:k*512] = r[uo+2*k:uo+2*k+2]
    si = fn = name = None
    a = struct.unpack_from('<H', r, 20)[0]
    while (t := struct.unpack_from('<I', r, a)[0]) != 0xFFFFFFFF:
        val = a + struct.unpack_from('<H', r, a+20)[0]
        if t == 0x10: si = struct.unpack_from('<Q', r, val)[0]
        if t == 0x30 and fn is None:
            fn = struct.unpack_from('<Q', r, val+8)[0]
            name = r[val+66 : val+66+2*r[val+64]].decode('utf-16-le')
        a += struct.unpack_from('<I', r, a+4)[0]
    return si, fn, name

checked = 0
for n in range(nrec):
    t = times(n)
    if not t or None in t: continue
    si, fn, name = t
    checked += 1
    flags = []
    if si < fn: flags.append('SI born before FN')
    if si % 10**7 == 0: flags.append('SI has zero fraction')
    if flags:
        print(f'record {n} "{name}": {", ".join(flags)}; gap {(fn - si) / 10**7 / 86400:.1f} days')
print(f'checked {checked} records')
blocks.caption: stomp_check.py: flag records whose SI creation time is earlier than FN creation, or has a zero sub-second fraction.

blocks.code:
$ python stomp_check.py ntfs.bin 1200
checked 928 records
$ python stomp_check.py ntfs_altered.bin 1200
record 41 "File.txt": SI born before FN, SI has zero fraction; gap 1168.6 days
checked 928 records
blocks.caption: Real output. ntfs_altered.bin is a copy of the test image in which we overwrote the SI created and modified times of record 41 with 2019-03-01 09:00:00 as a lab fixture.

blocks.md:
**Why those two checks.**

- *SI born before FN born.* Both are set when the file is created. If SI later claims an earlier birth, something rewrote SI. Benign causes exist (software restoring times), so you check what wrote it.
- *Zero fraction.* Times written by the file system normally carry a sub-second part. In the unaltered test image, none of the 928 records our script reaches (nor any of the 2,292 that dissect.ntfs reads) has an SI creation time with a zero fraction; our altered record does. A round number is a lead, nothing more: a careful tool can write any fraction.

**What a defender also checks**: the USN journal (BASIC_INFO_CHANGE records), `$LogFile`, process creation events, and Prefetch or Amcache entries for whatever tool made the change. ATT&CK's own analytic for this technique combines API use, command-line tools and SI versus FN mismatches.

blocks.prompt: An intruder used a kernel-level tool to make SI and FN agree on 2019. The comparison now shows nothing. What evidence could still contradict the 2019 date?
blocks.reveal:
Several things the tool did not touch:

- **The change journal** records the time change itself (BASIC_INFO_CHANGE), and any rename that moved FN, at the real time.
- **`$LogFile`** may still hold the recent metadata transaction.
- **Telemetry outside the disk**: process creation events, EDR records of the tool running, Prefetch for the tool.
- **Context**: a file claiming 2019 whose content refers to events from 2022.

Anti-forensics usually moves evidence rather than removing it.

blocks.md: One timestamp is a claim. Two attributes, a journal, a log and telemetry that agree are a finding. Write the finding with the corroboration, not the single field.

blocks.question: SI created = 2023-01-10 14:22:31.0000000, FN created = 2024-06-02 08:15:44.3871190. What is the most defensible statement?
options: SI created was probably rewritten after June 2024; corroborate with the USN journal and process telemetry before concluding
The file was created on 10 January 2023
The file was timestomped by the user who owns it
The FN time is wrong because FN is less reliable than SI
blocks.explain: SI earlier than FN plus a zero fraction is a strong lead that SI was rewritten, not proof of who did it or why. FN is the harder set to change, so the 2023 claim is the suspect one.

blocks.question: Why is last-access time weak evidence on NTFS?
options: It is stored only in FN, which users cannot see
Updates to it can be deferred by up to an hour and can be disabled entirely
It uses local time instead of UTC
It records the time the antivirus scanned the file
blocks.explain: Microsoft documents that NTFS may defer last-access updates by up to one hour and that the update can be turned off (disablelastaccess). It is a FILETIME in UTC and exists in SI too.

lessons.title: The USN change journal: a diary of every file change

blocks.md:
Backup and indexing software needs to know what changed without rescanning the disk. So NTFS keeps an **update sequence number (USN) change journal**: when any file or directory on the volume changes, the journal gets a record describing the change and the file's name ([Change Journals](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/change-journals)). For an investigator it is a diary of file activity, including files that no longer exist.

It is a metadata file named `$UsnJrnl` inside the `$Extend` folder, with a data stream named `$J` (the records, stored sparse, so the trimmed start reads as zeros) and a stream named `$Max` (settings such as the maximum size) ([libfsntfs notes](https://github.com/libyal/libfsntfs/blob/main/documentation/New%20Technologies%20File%20System%20%28NTFS%29.asciidoc)).

Each record is a `USN_RECORD_V2` ([Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winioctl/ns-winioctl-usn_record_v2)): record length, version, the file's reference (MFT record number plus sequence), the parent folder's reference, the USN (the record's offset in the journal), a FILETIME timestamp, a **reason** bit field, attributes and the file name. Reason flags you will use most:

- 0x100 FILE_CREATE, 0x200 FILE_DELETE
- 0x1 DATA_OVERWRITE, 0x2 DATA_EXTEND, 0x4 DATA_TRUNCATION
- 0x1000 RENAME_OLD_NAME, 0x2000 RENAME_NEW_NAME
- 0x8000 BASIC_INFO_CHANGE: attributes or *time stamps* changed
- 0x80000000 CLOSE

Reasons accumulate while a file is open, and closing writes a final record with CLOSE set. A rename or move writes two records, one with the old name and parent, one with the new.

blocks.title: How one file's life lands in the journal

scenes.caption: A program creates report.xlsx and writes to it. Each change appends a record; reasons accumulate until the file is closed.
Someone changes the file's timestamps. The journal records BASIC_INFO_CHANGE at the real time of the change, whatever value was written.
A rename writes two records, the old name then the new, and closing the file adds the usual CLOSE record. Now the journal links report.xlsx and svc_update.dat to the same MFT record.
Deletion: the journal records FILE_DELETE; the MFT record is marked free. Later the record may be reused, but the journal entries keep the names and times.

blocks.code:
import struct, sys
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
REASONS = {0x1: 'DATA_OVERWRITE', 0x2: 'DATA_EXTEND', 0x100: 'FILE_CREATE',
           0x200: 'FILE_DELETE', 0x1000: 'RENAME_OLD_NAME', 0x2000: 'RENAME_NEW_NAME',
           0x8000: 'BASIC_INFO_CHANGE', 0x80000000: 'CLOSE'}
buf = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
off = 0
while off < len(buf):
    (length, major, minor, ref, parent, usn, ts, reason,
     src, sec, attrs, nlen, noff) = struct.unpack_from('<IHHQQqqIIIIHH', buf, off)
    if length == 0: break                       # sparse padding
    name = buf[off+noff : off+noff+nlen].decode('utf-16-le')
    when = datetime(1601, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc) + timedelta(microseconds=ts // 10)
    entry, seq = ref & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF, ref >> 48
    why = '|'.join(v for k, v in REASONS.items() if reason & k)
    print(f'{when:%H:%M:%S} usn {usn:#x} MFT {entry}/{seq} {name:15} {why}')
    off += length

14:05:11 usn 0x2a6f058 MFT 1207/3 report.xlsx     DATA_EXTEND|FILE_CREATE
14:05:12 usn 0x2a6f0b0 MFT 1207/3 report.xlsx     DATA_EXTEND|FILE_CREATE|CLOSE
14:09:40 usn 0x2a6f108 MFT 1207/3 report.xlsx     BASIC_INFO_CHANGE
14:09:40 usn 0x2a6f160 MFT 1207/3 report.xlsx     BASIC_INFO_CHANGE|CLOSE
14:10:03 usn 0x2a6f1b8 MFT 1207/3 report.xlsx     RENAME_OLD_NAME
14:10:03 usn 0x2a6f210 MFT 1207/3 svc_update.dat  RENAME_NEW_NAME
14:10:03 usn 0x2a6f268 MFT 1207/3 svc_update.dat  RENAME_NEW_NAME|CLOSE

blocks.caption: Real output on 9 synthetic records that our own script built with the USN_RECORD_V2 layout. Times are UTC.

blocks.md:
**Reading the story.** `report.xlsx` was created at 14:05:11, its times were changed at 14:09:40, it was renamed to `svc_update.dat` at 14:10:03 and deleted at 14:31:57. Even if the MFT record 1207 has since been reused (its sequence would then be higher than 3), the journal still holds both names.

**Limits.** The journal has a target maximum size: at NTFS checkpoints, once it exceeds MaximumSize plus AllocationDelta, it is trimmed from the beginning ([Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/creating-modifying-and-deleting-a-change-journal)). How far back it reaches depends on how busy the volume is, so record the first USN and its time. An administrator can also delete the journal; Microsoft notes this resets the USN of every file to zero, which is itself a visible trace (lesson 15).

**Companion: `$LogFile`**, the NTFS metadata transaction journal used for crash recovery. It holds recent low-level metadata operations; MFTECmd parses both `$J` and `$LogFile`. On a live host, Velociraptor's `Windows.Forensics.Usn` artifact reads the journal across a fleet.

blocks.question: A file was renamed once. Why do you find two journal records with the same file reference at the same moment?
options: NTFS writes every record twice for safety
One record is in the J stream and its copy is in the Max stream
The second record is the CLOSE of the first
A rename or move writes one record with the old name and parent and one with the new
blocks.explain: Microsoft documents that a rename or move generates two USN records: RENAME_OLD_NAME with the old parent, RENAME_NEW_NAME with the new. The Max stream holds settings, not records.

blocks.question: The oldest record in a server's change journal is from three days ago. Your intrusion window starts two weeks ago. What do you write?
options: No files were changed before three days ago
The intruder deleted the journal
The journal does not cover the window; absence of earlier records says nothing about earlier activity
The server was rebuilt three days ago
blocks.explain: The journal is trimmed from the start once it exceeds its maximum size, so on a busy volume coverage is short. Deletion or a rebuild would need other evidence (for example a USN reset or a process event).

lessons.title: Linux ext4: superblock, inodes, extents and the journal

blocks.md:
**ext4** is the Linux file system that succeeded ext2 and ext3. The prereq showed timestamps through `stat`; here we read them from the disk, where an image puts them.

The layout, from the Linux kernel's documentation ([block groups](https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/ext4/blockgroup.html)): the volume is divided into **block groups**. In group 0 the first 1,024 bytes are left free for an x86 boot sector, then comes the **superblock** (volume-wide settings: magic number 0xEF53 at offset 0x38, block size as 2 to the power of 10 plus `s_log_block_size`, inodes per group, inode size). Group descriptors follow; each points to its group's bitmaps and **inode table**.

An **inode** (index node) is the per-file metadata record, numbered from 1. Inode N lives at position N minus 1 in the table. Lesson 4's MFT record is NTFS's counterpart.

blocks.title: One ext4 inode, field by field (inode 12, xattr_cap)

scenes.caption: The first bytes of a 128-byte inode: mode (file type and permissions) and size, then the times (shown as minutes:seconds after 12:00 UTC).
atime and mtime are 12:15:58. ctime is 12:16:08, ten seconds later: the inode itself changed after the content was written (for this test file, plausibly when its extended attribute was added).
dtime is 0: never deleted. On deletion ext4 sets dtime and frees the inode; the inode bitmap marks it free.
i_block begins with the extent header F30A; this empty file has 0 extents. A 128-byte inode ends soon after: no crtime field exists to read.

blocks.code:
import struct, sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
img = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
sb = img[1024:2048]                                   # superblock: byte 1024
magic = struct.unpack_from('<H', sb, 0x38)[0]
bsize = 1024 << struct.unpack_from('<I', sb, 0x18)[0]
ipg   = struct.unpack_from('<I', sb, 0x28)[0]         # inodes per group
isz   = struct.unpack_from('<H', sb, 0x58)[0]         # bytes per inode
print(f'magic {magic:#06x}, {bsize}-byte blocks, {isz}-byte inodes, {ipg} inodes/group')
gdt = (2 if bsize == 1024 else 1) * bsize             # group descriptor table
table = struct.unpack_from('<I', img, gdt + 8)[0]     # bg_inode_table_lo, group 0

def utc(sec): return datetime.fromtimestamp(sec, timezone.utc).strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')

for n in (11, 12, 13):                                # inodes start at 1
    r = img[table*bsize + (n-1)*isz : table*bsize + n*isz]
    mode, size = struct.unpack_from('<HxxI', r, 0)
    atime, ctime, mtime, dtime = struct.unpack_from('<4I', r, 0x08)
    eh_magic, eh_entries = struct.unpack_from('<HH', r, 0x28)   # i_block
    print(f'inode {n}: mode {mode:o}, {size} B, extents {eh_entries} (magic {eh_magic:#06x})')
    print(f'   m {utc(mtime)}  c {utc(ctime)}  a {utc(atime)}  dtime {dtime}')
    if isz >= 160:
        print('   crtime', utc(struct.unpack_from('<I', r, 0x90)[0]))
blocks.caption: ext4_inodes.py: read the superblock and three inodes straight from an image. Test image: ext4.bin, published as test data by Fox-IT's dissect.extfs project.
Real output (UTC). This image uses 128-byte inodes, so there is no creation time to report.

blocks.md:
**Deletion on ext4.** Portland State University course notes: on deletion the inode is marked free in the inode bitmap, `dtime` is set, the data blocks are not overwritten, and ext4 by default zeroes the block pointers in the inode ([PSU notes](https://web.cecs.pdx.edu/~dmcgrath/courses/Su26/forensics/ext.html)). Following the metadata to the old content, the FAT and NTFS trick, mostly fails. Two routes remain:

- **The journal.** ext4 journals through jbd2 (its journal layer). By default (`data=ordered`) only *metadata* goes through the journal ([kernel: journal](https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/ext4/journal.html)), so the journal can still hold an older copy of the block containing the inode, with its block map intact; if the transaction is still there, the pointers can be reconstructed (same notes). Tools such as ext4magic work this way (same notes); success depends on how much was written since, as the journal is reused.
- **Carving** the unallocated blocks (lesson 9).

`dtime` set and the inode free in the bitmap is your sign a file was deleted, and when.

Collect timestamps from the image, not from a mounted copy: mounting read-write can change atime and the journal, and the classic `stat()` call does not return crtime (the newer `statx()` call, Linux 4.11 and later, can report it as a birth time).

blocks.question: An ext4 image has 128-byte inodes. A colleague asks for each file's creation time. What do you answer?
options: 128-byte inodes have no creation time field; use other sources (journal, logs, application data) for when files appeared
Read crtime at offset 0x90
Use ctime, which is the creation time
Use dtime, which records the first write
blocks.explain: crtime exists only in the larger inode format. ctime is the inode change time, not creation (the prereq's backdating trick relies on that difference), and dtime is deletion time.

blocks.question: With the default data=ordered journal mode, what can the ext4 journal give you after a file is deleted?
options: Possibly an older copy of the metadata block holding the file's inode, with its extents
A full copy of the file's content
Nothing, because the journal is erased on deletion
The user name of whoever deleted it
blocks.explain: data=ordered sends metadata, not file data, through the journal. Older inode blocks in the journal can point recovery tools to the content blocks. ext4 does not log who deleted a file.

blocks.md:
**APFS** (Apple File System) is the default file system on Apple platforms and the successor to HFS Plus ([Apple File System Reference](https://developer.apple.com/support/downloads/Apple-File-System-Reference.pdf)). Two ideas from Apple's reference change how you examine a Mac or an iPhone:

- **Containers and volumes.** An APFS partition holds one *container*, which manages space and crash protection, and the container holds up to 100 *volumes* that share its free space. The container superblock's magic is `NXSB`, which Apple says it chose because it reads as an abbreviation of "NX superblock" in hex dumps.
- **Copy-on-write.** Modified objects are written to a new location instead of overwriting the old one, and the container records periodic *checkpoints*. Old versions are not destroyed by the act of changing them.

**Snapshots** follow from copy-on-write. Apple defines them as a stable, read-only copy of the file system at a point in time, fast and cheap to create (deleting one is more work). Each snapshot keeps the blocks it references alive. For an examiner: a file deleted after a snapshot was taken is still readable inside that snapshot.

APFS timestamps count **nanoseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC**.

**Encryption is the default.** On Macs with Apple silicon or an Apple T2 Security Chip, every APFS volume is created with a volume encryption key, and key handling happens in the Secure Enclave (a separate security processor). With FileVault (macOS full-volume encryption) on, the user's password is needed too, and moving the drive to another computer does not help ([Apple Platform Security](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/volume-encryption-with-filevault-sec4c6dc1b6e/web)). A raw image of such a drive without credentials is ciphertext: plan acquisition from the running, unlocked system (lesson 14).

blocks.title: Copy-on-write: why a snapshot keeps an old version alive

scenes.caption: The live file system's tree points to block 100, which holds version 1 of the file.
A snapshot is taken: it records the same tree. Both views now reference block 100.
The file is edited. Copy-on-write puts version 2 in a new block, 205, and the live tree moves to it. Block 100 is untouched.
The file is deleted from the live volume. The snapshot still references block 100, so version 1 survives until the snapshot is deleted.

blocks.code:
import struct, sys
from dissect.apfs import APFS              # Fox-IT's open-source APFS parser
raw = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read(4096)
magic, bsize, bcount = struct.unpack_from('<4sIQ', raw, 32)   # nx_superblock_t
print(f'{magic.decode()}: {bsize}-byte blocks, {bsize*bcount // 2**20} MiB container')

vol = APFS(open(sys.argv[1], 'rb')).volumes[0]
print(f'volume "{vol.name}": {len(vol.snapshots)} snapshots')
print('live volume root:', sorted(vol.get('/').listdir()))
for i in (0, 1, 511):
    snap = vol.snapshots[i]
    data = snap.open().get('/file').open().read()  # same path, older state
    print(f'{snap.name:13} taken {snap.create_time:%H:%M:%S.%f}  '
          f'/file = {data[:12]!r}')

volume "Snapshots": 512 snapshots
live volume root: ['.fseventsd']
Snapshot 0    taken 10:55:35.282069  /file = b'Snapshot 0\n'

blocks.md:
**What this means in practice.**

- Enumerate snapshots before concluding a file never existed; examine each as its own point in time.
- Snapshot creation times give you a ladder of states: our 512 snapshots span 10:55:35 to 10:58:18.
- Copy-on-write also leaves older metadata in earlier checkpoints, which specialised tools can use, but do not promise it: space is reused once nothing references it.
- On iPhones and Apple silicon Macs the useful acquisition is almost always logical (from the unlocked system), so these structures reach you through an extraction tool rather than a raw image.

blocks.question: A suspect deleted a document from their Mac at 15:00. The volume has a snapshot from 14:30. What can you expect?
options: Nothing: APFS overwrites deleted files immediately
The document is in the snapshot only if it was saved after 15:00
The 14:30 snapshot still contains the document as it was at 14:30
Snapshots hold only metadata, never file content
blocks.explain: A snapshot is a read-only copy of the file system at its creation time and keeps referenced blocks alive. Later deletion from the live volume does not touch it.

blocks.question: You remove the internal SSD from an Apple silicon Mac with FileVault on and image it with a write-blocker. What do you have?
options: A readable APFS volume, because write-blockers bypass encryption
Encrypted data that stays unreadable without valid credentials or a recovery key
A blank image, because the SSD erases itself
A readable image as long as you image the whole container
blocks.explain: Apple documents that internal APFS volumes stay encrypted without valid login credentials or a cryptographic recovery key, even attached to another computer. A write-blocker preserves data; it does not decrypt it.

lessons.title: Carving: recovering files with no metadata at all

blocks.md:
When the metadata is gone (ext4 nulled the pointers, the MFT record was reused, the volume was reformatted), you can still look for the content itself. The CyBOK Forensics knowledge area (the UK-funded Cyber Security Body of Knowledge) defines **file carving** as recovering and reconstructing file content directly from block storage without using the file system metadata ([CyBOK](https://www.cybok.org/media/downloads/Forensics_v1.0.1.pdf)).

It rests on two observations: most file formats have fixed beginning and end markers (a *header* and a *footer*), and file systems favour sequential layout. JPEG images start with the bytes FF D8 FF and end with FF D9. The basic algorithm: scan for a header, scan on for the footer, copy what is between.

blocks.title: Carving a JPEG out of raw sectors

scenes.caption: Raw bytes from unallocated space. No name, no size, no directory entry: just bytes. (Excerpt; offsets abbreviated.)
Scan for FF D8 FF. Found at byte 1,099,264 of the disk, sector 2,147: a JPEG probably starts here.
Scan on for FF D9. Found 1,174 bytes after the start.
Copy header through footer and hash it: the SHA-256 matches the photo recovered through the FAT entry in lesson 3. Two independent methods, one answer.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, sys
img = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
HEAD, FOOT = b'\xff\xd8\xff', b'\xff\xd9'      # JPEG start and end markers
pos, found = 0, 0
while (start := img.find(HEAD, pos)) != -1:
    end = img.find(FOOT, start)
    if end == -1: break
    blob = img[start:end + 2]                   # header .. footer inclusive
    found += 1
    print(f'jpeg #{found}: offset {start} (sector {start // 512}), '
          f'{len(blob)} bytes, sha256 {hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest()[:16]}')
    pos = end + 2
print('done,', found, 'candidate(s)')
blocks.caption: carve.py: a minimal header and footer carver for JPEG.

blocks.code:
$ python carve.py disk.img
jpeg #1: offset 1099264 (sector 2147), 1174 bytes, sha256 fb067d78afd6c66a
done, 1 candidate(s)
blocks.caption: Real output on the lab disk from lesson 3. The hash equals the original photo's (fb067d78afd6c66a).

blocks.md:
**Where simple carving breaks** (CyBOK's catalogue of layouts):

- **Contiguous**: the usual case, and the one above.
- **Nested**: one file's bytes inside another's. JPEGs commonly embed a thumbnail, itself a JPEG, so a naive carver stops at the thumbnail's FF D9 and returns a truncated image.
- **Bifragmented** and **interleaved**: the file is split, or two files alternate. Header and footer carving returns garbage; better carvers validate the format's internal structure.

**Tools.** PhotoRec (by Christophe Grenier, GPL) ignores the file system and goes after the underlying data, opens media read-only and knows over 480 file extensions ([PhotoRec](https://www.cgsecurity.org/wiki/PhotoRec)). Foremost carves by headers, footers and file structure ([Kali](https://www.kali.org/tools/foremost/)). bulk_extractor, by Simson Garfinkel, scans raw data without parsing the file system and extracts structured features such as email addresses, credit card numbers, JPEGs and JSON snippets, with histograms of what it finds ([bulk_extractor](https://github.com/simsong/bulk_extractor)).

**SSDs change the odds.** Solid-state drives must erase blocks before reuse, so the TRIM and UNMAP commands (added to the ATA and SCSI drive command sets respectively) let the file system tell the drive which blocks are free. Windows calls this *delete notification* and enables it by default on NTFS ([fsutil behavior](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/fsutil-behavior)). CyBOK summarises experiments by C. King and T. Vidas (at DFRWS 2011, the Digital Forensics Research Workshop): on a TRIM-aware OS (Windows 7 and later) recovery rates were almost universally zero, against near-perfect recovery under Windows XP. Graeme Bell and Richard Boddington of Murdoch University, Perth, had warned in 2010 that SSDs can destroy evidence on their own, without instructions from the computer ([JDFSL](https://commons.erau.edu/jdfsl/vol5/iss3/1/)).

Practical consequence: on a modern SSD, deleted-file recovery is the exception, so the artefacts *about* files (journals, logs, LNK files, registry) carry more weight.
A carved file has no name, no path, no timestamps and no owner. You can testify that these bytes were on the disk at this offset. Who created them, and when, needs other evidence.

blocks.question: Your carver recovers a 9 KB JPEG that opens as a tiny 160 x 120 picture, while the camera wrote 4 MB images. What most likely happened?
options: The camera compressed the image after deletion
TRIM shrank the file
The JPEG header was corrupted
The carver stopped at the FF D9 of an embedded thumbnail (nested content)
blocks.explain: JPEGs commonly carry a thumbnail that is itself a complete JPEG. A header and footer carver that stops at the first FF D9 returns the thumbnail. TRIM discards blocks; it does not shrink files.

blocks.question: Why does carving deleted files from a Windows 11 laptop's NVMe SSD usually fail?
options: NVMe drives do not use sectors
With delete notifications (TRIM) on by default, the drive is told freed blocks are unused and typically clears them
Windows 11 encrypts deleted files with a separate key
Carving only works on FAT
blocks.explain: Delete notification tells the drive which clusters were freed, and the drive's garbage collection makes them read back empty. CyBOK cites near-zero recovery on TRIM-aware systems. Carving is file system independent, and NVMe still exposes blocks.

lessons.title: The registry in depth, and proving a USB drive was used

blocks.md:
Every key also has a **last write time**, the last time the key or any of its values was modified ([RegQueryInfoKey](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winreg/nf-winreg-regqueryinfokeyw)). It belongs to the key, not to each value, so it says *something under this key changed then*.

**Tools.** Eric Zimmerman's free tools include Registry Explorer (a viewer that searches across hives and handles locked files) and RECmd (its command-line twin) ([list](https://ericzimmerman.github.io/)).

**USB storage.** When a device is plugged in, the Plug and Play (PnP) manager identifies it by a *device instance ID* built from its vendor ID (VID), product ID (PID) and, if it has one, its serial number, for example `USB\VID_045E&PID_0840\0C33CG9212501N0` ([Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/usbcon/usb-device-specific-registry-settings)). A device with no usable serial gets an ID derived from the port instead, so the same stick on another port looks like a new device.

Oleg Afonin of ElcomSoft (a forensic software vendor) describes the main places this lands ([ElcomSoft, 2026](https://blog.elcomsoft.com/2026/02/usb-device-forensics-on-windows-10-and-11/)):

- `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR`: storage devices Windows has enumerated, by product, then serial. If the serial's second character is `&`, Windows probably generated it.
- Under each device's `Properties\{83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a1923f573b29}`, timestamps that in many builds mean: 0x64 last driver install, 0x65 first install, 0x66 last arrival (plugged in), 0x67 last removal.

More witnesses:

- `setupapi.dev.log` in `%SystemRoot%\inf` is the plain-text device installation log written by the PnP manager and SetupAPI, one section per installation ([Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/install/setupapi-text-logs)). It helps date the first time a device was set up.
- The `Microsoft-Windows-Partition/Diagnostic` event log's event 1006 can include a copy of the device's volume boot record, from which the **volume serial number** (VSN) can be read: at offset 0x48 on NTFS, 0x43 on FAT32, 0x64 on exFAT ([ElcomSoft](https://blog.elcomsoft.com/2026/02/usb-device-forensics-on-windows-10-and-11/)). On FAT16, Microsoft's on-disk format puts the same field (`BS_VolID`) at byte 39. ElcomSoft notes major Windows updates may clear this log.

The VSN is the bridge: shortcut files record the VSN of the volume a file was opened from (next lesson). Match the two and you tie a document to a physical drive.

blocks.title: From a USB stick to a document: the correlation chain

nodes.label:
LNK in Recent
volume serial + path

scenes.caption: Start with the physical exhibit: a seized USB stick, its serial reported in its USB descriptor, and its FAT volume with serial 1234-ABCD.
The SYSTEM hive's USBSTOR key lists the stick's serial, with first install, last arrival and last removal times.
setupapi.dev.log dates the first installation independently. Two sources, one device.
Partition/Diagnostic event 1006 holds the boot record seen when it was mounted, giving the VSN 1234-ABCD.
A shortcut file in the user's Recent folder records a document opened from a removable volume with VSN 1234-ABCD. The chain now runs from the exhibit to a file and a user profile.

blocks.code:
import struct, sys
def vsn_from_vbr(vbr):
    """Volume serial number from a volume boot record (first sector of a volume)."""
    if vbr[3:11] == b'NTFS    ':  off = 0x48          # NTFS: 8 bytes, Windows shows the low 4
    elif vbr[82:90] == b'FAT32   ': off = 0x43
    elif vbr[3:11] == b'EXFAT   ': off = 0x64         # exFAT ('EXFAT   ' at byte 3)
    elif vbr[54:59] == b'FAT16' or vbr[54:59] == b'FAT12': off = 0x27
    else: return None
    v = struct.unpack_from('<I', vbr, off)[0]
    return f'{v >> 16:04X}-{v & 0xFFFF:04X}'

disk = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
start = struct.unpack_from('<I', disk, 446 + 8)[0]     # first partition's start LBA
vbr = disk[start*512 : start*512 + 512]
mine = vsn_from_vbr(vbr)
print('VSN on the seized USB drive :', mine)
print('VSN recorded in the LNK file:', sys.argv[2])
print('unknown file system: no verdict' if mine is None
      else 'match' if mine == sys.argv[2] else 'no match')
blocks.caption: vsn_match.py: read a volume serial number from a boot record and compare it with the one in a shortcut file. Offsets: NTFS, FAT32 and exFAT from ElcomSoft, FAT12/16 from Microsoft's FAT format description.

blocks.code:
$ python vsn_match.py disk.img 1234-ABCD
VSN on the seized USB drive : 1234-ABCD
VSN recorded in the LNK file: 1234-ABCD
match
blocks.caption: Real output on our lab disk (the drive), with the serial taken from the LNK file parsed in the next lesson.

blocks.md: A VSN changes when a volume is reformatted and is only 32 bits on FAT, so a match is strong corroboration, not a unique fingerprint. Combine it with the device serial and times. The meanings of the 0x64 to 0x67 properties also vary by Windows build: test on a reference system before testifying to them.

blocks.question: A USBSTOR entry's serial is `7&2a4d1f0&0`. What does that suggest?
options: The serial was probably generated by Windows from the port, so it may not identify this device uniquely across machines
The device is a phone, not a storage device
The device was encrypted with BitLocker To Go
The device was connected seven times
blocks.explain: ElcomSoft's heuristic: a second character of & suggests a Windows-generated ID because the device lacked a unique serial. Microsoft documents that such IDs are tied to the port.

blocks.question: A registry key's last write time is 2026-03-02 14:28. Which statement is safe?
options: Every value under this key was written at 14:28
A user opened this key in regedit at 14:28
The key or at least one of its values was last modified at 14:28
The key was created at 14:28
blocks.explain: Microsoft defines it as the last time the key or any of its values was modified. It is per key, not per value, and it records modification, not viewing or creation.

lessons.title: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin

blocks.md:
When a user opens a document, Windows quietly writes down where it was. These records survive after the document, and even the drive it lived on, are gone.

**LNK files** (shell links, the format of Windows shortcuts, named for their `.lnk` extension) are specified by Microsoft in MS-SHLLINK ([ShellLinkHeader](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-shllink/c3376b21-0931-45e4-b2fc-a48ac0e60d15)). The header is exactly 0x4C bytes, carries the class identifier `00021401-0000-0000-C000-000000000046`, and stores the **target's** creation, access and write times (FILETIME, UTC) and size. An optional LinkInfo block holds a VolumeID with the drive type (for example DRIVE_REMOVABLE), the volume serial number and label, plus the local path ([VolumeID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-shllink/b7b3eea7-dbff-4275-bd58-83ba3f12d87a)).

Windows keeps such shortcuts in each user's `AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent` folder ([libyal](https://github.com/libyal/dtformats/blob/main/documentation/Jump%20lists%20format.asciidoc)).

blocks.code:
import struct, sys, uuid
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
DRIVE = {2: 'REMOVABLE', 3: 'FIXED', 4: 'REMOTE', 5: 'CDROM'}
def filetime(v):
    return f'{datetime(1601, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc) + timedelta(microseconds=v // 10):%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}'
b = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
size, clsid, flags, attrs, ctime, atime, wtime, fsize = struct.unpack_from('<I16sIIQQQI', b, 0)
assert size == 0x4C and uuid.UUID(bytes_le=clsid) == uuid.UUID('00021401-0000-0000-c000-000000000046')
print('target created ', filetime(ctime))
print('target accessed', filetime(atime))
print('target written ', filetime(wtime))
print('target size    ', fsize, 'bytes')
off = 0x4C
if flags & 0x1:                                   # HasLinkTargetIDList: skip it
    off += 2 + struct.unpack_from('<H', b, off)[0]
if flags & 0x2:                                   # HasLinkInfo
    li = off
    _, _, liflags, voff, boff = struct.unpack_from('<IIIII', b, li)
    if liflags & 1:                               # VolumeIDAndLocalBasePath
        _, dtype, serial, loff = struct.unpack_from('<IIII', b, li + voff)
        label = b[li+voff+loff:].split(b'\0')[0].decode()
        path = b[li+boff:].split(b'\0')[0].decode()
        print(f'drive type      {DRIVE.get(dtype, dtype)}, label "{label}"')
        print(f'volume serial   {serial >> 16:04X}-{serial & 0xFFFF:04X}')
        print('local path     ', path)
blocks.caption: lnk_parse.py: parse the LNK header and the LinkInfo VolumeID, following MS-SHLLINK.

blocks.code:
$ python lnk_parse.py payroll_export.csv.lnk
target created  2026-03-02 13:58:20
target accessed 2026-03-02 14:20:41
target written  2026-03-02 14:01:07
target size     48213 bytes
drive type      REMOVABLE, label "EVIDENCE"
volume serial   1234-ABCD
local path      E:\Q3\payroll_export.csv
blocks.caption: Real output on a shortcut we built ourselves to the MS-SHLLINK layout; the times, size and path are synthetic. The serial matches our lab USB volume from lessons 3 and 10.

blocks.md:
Never confuse two sets of times: those *inside* the LNK describe the target (here created 13:58:20, written 14:01:07). The LNK file's own times say when the shortcut was created and last updated; examiners read them as the first and last time the target was opened through this account, and confirm with Jump Lists.

**Jump Lists** (a taskbar feature since Windows 7) keep per-application recent items ([libyal](https://github.com/libyal/dtformats/blob/main/documentation/Jump%20lists%20format.asciidoc)). In `Recent\AutomaticDestinations`, each `.automaticDestinations-ms` file is an OLE (Object Linking and Embedding) Compound File (a little file system inside a file) holding a `DestList` stream plus one embedded LNK stream per item. DestList entries record the host name, an entry number, a last modification time, pin status and the path. The file name begins with an application ID derived from the program's path, so you know which program opened what. JLECmd parses them.

**ShellBags.** Explorer stores folder view settings in `BagMRU` keys in `NTUSER.DAT` and `UsrClass.dat`, which is why investigators use them to recover folder navigation history ([Velociraptor artifact](https://docs.velociraptor.app/artifact_references/pages/windows.forensics.shellbags/)). Vincent Lo's SANS paper warns that many activities change ShellBag timestamps and that the structure varies by Windows version ([SANS, 2014](https://www.sans.org/white-papers/34545/)): treat their times with care. ShellBags Explorer and SBECmd parse them.

**Recycle Bin.** Deleting through Explorer moves a file into the `$Recycle.Bin` folder at the root of the drive, in a subfolder named after the user's SID (security identifier), as a pair: a `$R` file with the content and a `$I` file with the format version, original size, deletion time (FILETIME) and original path ([libyal](https://github.com/libyal/dtformats/blob/main/documentation/Windows%20Recycle.Bin%20file%20formats.asciidoc)). The SID folder tells you whose bin it was. RBCmd parses them.
