A shortcut appears in Recent: target times, size, drive type REMOVABLE, VSN 1234-ABCD, path.
The program's Jump List gains a DestList entry and an embedded LNK, with its own last modification time.
Browsing to the folder updated ShellBags in UsrClass.dat: proof the user navigated to `E:\Q3`.
Meanwhile the device itself left USBSTOR and setupapi entries (lesson 10). Each artefact answers a different question: which file, which program, which folder, which device.

blocks.md: These artefacts show that a *user account* interacted with a file, a folder or a drive. They are strongest together and with the drive in hand.

blocks.question: An LNK file in Recent says its target was written 2026-03-02 14:01:07. The LNK file itself was created 2026-03-04 09:12. What can you say?
options: The target was modified on 4 March
The LNK file is forged because its dates disagree
The target was deleted on 4 March
When the shortcut was last updated, the target's write time was 2 March 14:01:07; the user most likely first opened it through this account on 4 March
blocks.explain: Header times describe the target as it was when the link was last updated; the LNK's own creation time reflects when the shortcut was made. Different dates are normal, not a sign of forgery.

blocks.question: The USB stick is lost. What can still show that the user browsed its folder `E:\Q3`?
options: Only the stick itself
The master file table of the laptop's C: drive
SRUM
ShellBags in the user's hives, and LNK and Jump List entries pointing to `E:\Q3`
blocks.explain: ShellBags record navigated folders, and LNK and Jump List entries record opened files with their paths and volume serial, all stored on the laptop. The laptop's C: MFT does not index files on E:.

lessons.title: SRUM and browser history: network use and what was visited

blocks.md:
Two more databases answer *which program moved data* and *what the user looked at*.

**SRUM** (System Resource Usage Monitor) is a Windows database at `C:\Windows\System32\sru\SRUDB.dat`, stored in ESE (the Extensible Storage Engine, Microsoft's embedded database engine; [Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/extensible-storage-engine/extensible-storage-engine)). Velociraptor's SRUM artifact extracts its Execution Stats, Application Resource Usage, Network Connections and Network Usage tables; Network Usage rows carry BytesSent and BytesRecvd per application and user ([Velociraptor](https://docs.velociraptor.app/artifact_references/pages/windows.forensics.srum/)). SrumECmd processes SRUDB.dat together with the SOFTWARE hive. In an exfiltration case, SRUM can say *chrome.exe under this account sent this many bytes* in a period, even after the browser history was cleared.

**Browser history** lives in SQLite databases in the user's profile. Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge) keep a file named `History` with tables including `urls` (url, title, visit_count, typed_count, last_visit_time) and `visits` (one row per visit, with visit_time); Velociraptor's Chrome artifact queries exactly these ([Velociraptor](https://docs.velociraptor.app/artifact_references/pages/windows.applications.chrome.history/)).

Two epochs to know:

- Chromium time is **microseconds since 1 January 1601 UTC** (the Windows epoch), per Chromium's own `base/time/time.h` ([source](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/base/time/time.h)). The gap to the Unix epoch is 11,644,473,600 seconds.
- Firefox's `places.sqlite` uses PRTime, **microseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC** ([NSPR](https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/nspr/reference/prtime.html)).

So 13416934350000000 in Chrome and 1772460750000000 in Firefox are the same instant: 2026-03-02 14:12:30 UTC.

blocks.code:
import sqlite3, sys
db = sqlite3.connect(f'file:{sys.argv[1]}?mode=ro', uri=True)   # read-only
# Chromium stores microseconds since 1601-01-01 UTC; 11644473600 s separate 1601 and 1970
q = '''SELECT datetime(v.visit_time / 1000000 - 11644473600, 'unixepoch') AS utc,
              u.url, u.title, u.visit_count, u.typed_count
       FROM visits v JOIN urls u ON u.id = v.url ORDER BY v.visit_time'''
for row in db.execute(q):
    print(' | '.join(map(str, row)))
blocks.caption: chrome_history.py: list visits from a copy of a Chromium History database, opened read-only, converting times to UTC.

blocks.code:
$ python chrome_history.py History
2026-03-02 13:51:09 | https://mail.example.com/inbox | Inbox | 3 | 1
2026-03-02 14:12:30 | https://files.example.net/upload | Upload a file | 1 | 1
2026-03-02 14:28:02 | https://www.example.org/how-to-clear-usb-history | How to clear USB history | 1 | 0
blocks.caption: Real output on a small History database we built with the same table and column names; the visits are synthetic and use example domains.

blocks.md:
**Collection notes.**

- Copy the database *with* its `-wal` and `-shm` files. In SQLite's write-ahead log mode, new changes are appended to the WAL file and moved into the main file at a checkpoint ([SQLite](https://sqlite.org/wal.html)), so recent visits may exist only in the WAL.
- Always work on a copy and open it read-only; opening a live database in a normal client can trigger a checkpoint and change the evidence.
- Deleted rows can linger in free pages inside SQLite files; specialised tools recover them, which is another form of carving.

blocks.title: One afternoon, three sources on one axis (synthetic case, UTC)

scenes.caption: Minutes after 13:45. Browser: webmail at 13:51. Nothing unusual yet.
LNK target times: payroll_export.csv created on the USB stick at 13:58, written at 14:01.
Browser: a file upload page at 14:12. The question becomes: what was uploaded, and how much?
SRUM: a Network Usage row for the browser under this account in that period, with bytes sent. It cannot name the file, but it sizes the transfer. (Illustrative position.)
Browser: a search on how to clear USB history at 14:28. Not proof of anything alone, but it speaks to intent, and it tells you to look hard for cleanup (lesson 15).

blocks.question: A Chrome visit_time is 13416934350000000. Which conversion gives the Unix time in seconds?
blocks.explain: Chromium counts microseconds since 1601, so divide by one million and subtract the 11,644,473,600 seconds between 1601 and 1970. Dividing by ten million would be FILETIME's 100 ns ticks; skipping the subtraction gives a date in 2395.

blocks.question: The suspect cleared their browser history. What can SRUM still offer?
options: Per-application, per-user network byte counts with timestamps, showing that the browser moved data
The URLs that were visited
The content of the uploaded file
Nothing, because clearing history also clears SRUM
blocks.explain: SRUM's Network Usage table records BytesSent and BytesRecvd per application and user. It does not record URLs or content, and the browser's clear-history function does not touch SRUDB.dat.

lessons.title: Mobile forensics: extraction levels, encryption and isolation

blocks.md:
Phones hold much of a person's digital life, and they are built so that the approach of this course so far (pull the storage, image it, parse it) rarely works.

NIST SP 800-101 Revision 1 ([Guidelines on Mobile Device Forensics, 2014](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-101r1.pdf)) classifies extraction methods in five levels, a pyramid NIST attributes to Sam Brothers (2008), a US Customs and Border Protection examiner and one of the guide's authors. Going up, methods become more technical, invasive, time consuming and expensive.

1. **Manual extraction**: photographing what the screen shows by using the phone's interface. Deleted data cannot be recovered at this level.
2. **Logical extraction**: connecting over USB or a wireless link and asking the phone for its data. The most used level; the protocol chosen can change data (for example marking unread SMS as read).
3. **Hex dumping and JTAG**: a physical acquisition of memory in place. JTAG (Joint Test Action Group, a hardware test and debug interface) gives raw flash access.
4. **Chip-off**: removing the flash chip and reading it; the wear-levelling layout must be reverse engineered.
5. **Micro read**: examining the gates of the chip under an electron microscope; reserved, NIST says, for cases on the scale of a national security crisis.

blocks.title: NIST SP 800-101r1 extraction levels (rank, not measured cost)

scenes.caption: Level 1 to level 5 by rank on NIST's scale: higher means more technical, invasive, time consuming and expensive.
Day-to-day casework lives at level 2: logical extraction through the phone's own interfaces.
Levels 3 to 5 read physical storage. On modern phones that storage is encrypted with keys held in hardware, so a raw dump without the keys is ciphertext.

blocks.md:
**Encryption decides what any level can reach.**

- **iOS Data Protection** gives every new file its own 256-bit key and assigns the file to a class ([Apple](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/data-protection-classes-secb010e978a/web)): Class A *Complete Protection* (key discarded shortly after lock: 10 seconds when Require Password is Immediately), Class B *Protected Unless Open*, Class C *Protected Until First User Authentication* (the default for third-party app data; the key stays in memory after the first unlock) and Class D *No Protection*.
- **Android file-based encryption (FBE)**, required for devices launching with Android 10 or later, splits storage into *credential encrypted* (CE) storage, available only after the user unlocks, and *device encrypted* (DE) storage, available during Direct Boot before unlock ([Android](https://source.android.com/docs/security/features/encryption/file-based)).

Examiners therefore speak of **BFU** (before first unlock: the phone was powered off or rebooted and the passcode not entered since) and **AFU** (after first unlock). ElcomSoft's work shows how little a BFU iPhone yields compared with AFU ([ElcomSoft](https://blog.elcomsoft.com/2019/12/bfu-extraction-forensic-analysis-of-locked-and-disabled-iphones/)).

blocks.code:
# Simplified model of iOS Data Protection classes (Apple Platform Security guide).
# Which class keys are in memory, and so which files are readable, in each state?
CLASSES = {
    'A Complete':                 lambda s: s == 'unlocked',
    'B Unless Open (open files)': lambda s: s == 'unlocked',   # simplified: new writes allowed when locked
    'C Until First User Auth':    lambda s: s in ('AFU locked', 'unlocked'),
    'D No Protection':            lambda s: True,
}
for state in ('BFU', 'AFU locked', 'unlocked'):
    readable = [name for name, ok in CLASSES.items() if ok(state)]
    print(f'{state:11} readable: {", ".join(readable)}')
blocks.caption: ios_classes.py: a deliberately simplified model of which Data Protection classes are readable in each state. Real devices have exceptions (for example Class B files already open when the phone locked).

blocks.code:
$ python ios_classes.py
BFU         readable: D No Protection
AFU locked  readable: C Until First User Auth, D No Protection
unlocked    readable: A Complete, B Unless Open (open files), C Until First User Auth, D No Protection
blocks.caption: Real output of the model.

blocks.md:
**Seizure and isolation.** NIST warns that phones can be reset remotely, so they must be isolated from networks; that Faraday containers (shielded bags) attenuate the signal but may not eliminate it, and an exposed cable can act as an antenna; and that devices can power off when the battery runs low ([SP 800-101r1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-101r1.pdf)). Given BFU and AFU, a phone that powers off or reboots in an evidence bag can lose most of what a lawful extraction could have read. Plan power and isolation together, under the legal authority you have.

**Extraction in practice.** Signal's 2021 analysis described UFED, the phone extraction product of the forensic vendor Cellebrite, as essentially a front end to `adb backup` (the backup command of the Android Debug Bridge, Android's developer connection tool) on Android and iTunes backup on iPhone, with Physical Analyzer parsing the result (lesson 16). Such routes narrow: since Android 12, `adb backup` leaves out data of apps that target Android 12 or later.

Turning a seized phone off "to preserve it" can move it from AFU to BFU and lock most of its data away for good. Decide on power, isolation and extraction before you touch it, and document every interaction.

blocks.question: A seized iPhone was found switched off and has not been unlocked since. Which data is most likely readable without the passcode?
options: Everything in Class C, because it is the default
Everything, because a chip-off bypasses Data Protection
Only data protected by Class D (No Protection) and similar always-available items
All messages, because the phone was off
blocks.explain: This is BFU: no class keys except D's are available. Class C keys appear only after the first unlock. Chip-off yields ciphertext, since keys are bound to the device's hardware.

blocks.question: Why does NIST caution that logical extraction may modify data?
options: The connection type and protocol used to talk to the phone can change data on it, for example marking unread SMS as read
Logical extraction always wipes the phone
Logical extraction writes a forensic agent into the bootloader
It uses JTAG, which resets memory
blocks.explain: SP 800-101r1 notes that different connection methods and protocols may modify data, giving unread SMS as the example. It does not wipe the phone, and JTAG is level 3, not logical.

lessons.title: Live acquisition and encryption: the Ross Ulbricht laptop (2013)

blocks.md:
The prereq's order of volatility said memory goes first. Full-disk encryption adds a harsher rule: **once a machine locks or powers off, the disk may become unreadable for good.** Sometimes the most important forensic act is keeping a computer awake.

**The case.** Silk Road was a dark-web drug marketplace run by an administrator called "Dread Pirate Roberts". On 1 October 2013, agents followed Ross Ulbricht to a public library in San Francisco's Glen Park neighbourhood ([Computerworld](https://www.computerworld.com/article/1617041/prosecution-silk-road-founder-caught-red-handed.html)). An undercover Homeland Security agent, Jared Der-Yeghiayan, chatting as the user "Cirrus", asked the administrator to log in and check something. Once Ulbricht had logged in, other agents moved in, took the laptop out of Ulbricht's reach and made the arrest; another agent photographed the screen ([KQED](https://www.kqed.org/news/12023762/2013-sf-sting-captured-ross-ulbricht-silk-road-operator-pardoned-by-trump)).

At the January 2015 trial, FBI computer scientist Thomas Kiernan testified about the laptop, a Samsung 700Z running Ubuntu Linux ([PCWorld](https://www.pcworld.com/article/2873572/prosecutors-tighten-case-against-alleged-silk-road-mastermind.html)). Kiernan also testified ([Vice](https://www.vice.com/en/article/prosecutors-in-silk-road-trial-present-damning-evidence-from-ross-ulbrichts-computer/)) that a male-female FBI team faked a domestic spat behind Ulbricht, drawing Ulbricht up from the seat; agents grabbed the computer while it was open and unencrypted; Kiernan kept it active for hours so it would not lock; it held chat logs, journal entries, expense reports and an apparent backup of the Silk Road site; and a private PGP key in a `keys` folder matched the public key posted on Silk Road.

Ulbricht got two life sentences plus 40 years; President Trump pardoned Ulbricht in January 2025 ([KQED](https://www.kqed.org/news/12023762/2013-sf-sting-captured-ross-ulbricht-silk-road-operator-pardoned-by-trump)). Forensically, the case turned on capturing a running, decrypted system.

blocks.title: Glen Park library, 1 October 2013 (simplified from trial reporting)

scenes.caption: The undercover agent, chatting as Cirrus, asks the site administrator to log in and check something.
Ulbricht logs in. The laptop is now unlocked, decrypted and showing the administrator's session.
A staged argument behind Ulbricht draws attention; agents move in and take the laptop out of reach before the lid can close. An agent photographs the screen.
Kiernan keeps the machine active for hours so it never relocks, then examines the decrypted contents: chats, journal, keys.

blocks.md:
**Live or dead acquisition?** A *dead* acquisition images a powered-off disk through a write-blocker: clean, repeatable, but useless if the volume is encrypted and you hold no key. A *live* acquisition works on the running system: it can copy the decrypted file system and memory, but every action changes the machine a little.

Recognise encryption before you decide. Most volumes announce themselves near their start: NTFS writes `NTFS` at byte 3 of its boot sector; a BitLocker volume writes `-FVE-FS-` there instead (FVE: full volume encryption) ([libfsntfs notes](https://github.com/libyal/libfsntfs/blob/main/documentation/New%20Technologies%20File%20System%20%28NTFS%29.asciidoc)); APFS shows `NXSB` even when its volumes are encrypted, because APFS encrypts per volume: check each volume superblock's `APFS_FS_UNENCRYPTED` flag ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/support/downloads/Apple-File-System-Reference.pdf)). ext4 shows 0xEF53. Data that matches no known signature and looks random is a strong hint of encryption.

blocks.code:
import sys
SIGS = [  # (offset, magic, meaning)
    (3,    b'NTFS    ', 'NTFS'),
    (3,    b'-FVE-FS-', 'BitLocker-encrypted volume'),
    (54,   b'FAT16   ', 'FAT16'),
    (82,   b'FAT32   ', 'FAT32'),
    (32,   b'NXSB',     'APFS container (volumes may be encrypted)'),
    (1080, b'\x53\xef', 'ext2/3/4 (superblock magic 0xEF53)'),
]
for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    with open(path, 'rb') as f:
        head = f.read(4096)
    kind = next((m for o, s, m in SIGS if head[o:o+len(s)] == s), 'unknown: check for encryption')
    print(f'{path:22} {kind}')
blocks.caption: what_volume.py: identify a volume by its signature. Run it on images or on a read-only device node.

blocks.code:
$ python what_volume.py usb_volume.img windows.img linux.img mac.img photo.jpg
usb_volume.img         FAT16
windows.img            NTFS
linux.img              ext2/3/4 (superblock magic 0xEF53)
mac.img                APFS container (volumes may be encrypted)
photo.jpg              unknown: check for encryption

blocks.md:
**A live acquisition plan, in order** (each step written in your notes with the time):

1. Prevent locking: keep the session active, do not close the lid, connect power.
2. Photograph the screen and what is running.
3. Capture memory (prereq tools), because keys and unlocked containers live there.
4. Copy the decrypted data you need: a logical image of mounted volumes, or a full image taken from the running system.
5. Record recovery keys if the law and your authority allow it.
6. Only then decide whether to shut down.

The ACPO guide's Principle 2 (ACPO: the Association of Chief Police Officers of England, Wales and Northern Ireland) applies directly: whoever must access original data has to be competent to do so and able to explain the relevance and implications of their actions ([ACPO v5](https://www.digital-detective.net/digital-forensics-documents/ACPO_Good_Practice_Guide_for_Digital_Evidence_v5.pdf)).
Encryption turns *keep it running* into the first forensic step. If you arrive at a decrypted, unlocked machine, you may never get that state back.

blocks.question: You arrive at a suspect's unlocked Windows laptop with a BitLocker-encrypted system drive. What should you avoid first?
options: Photographing the screen
Shutting it down to take a clean write-blocked image
Capturing memory
Connecting the power adapter
blocks.explain: A powered-off BitLocker drive is unreadable without a key, so shutting down first can destroy the only decrypted view. Photographing, connecting power and capturing memory preserve state.

blocks.question: A live acquisition inevitably changes the running system. Which ACPO principle governs this?
options: Principle 1: no action should change data that may be relied on in court, so live acquisition is forbidden
Principle 3: only a second examiner may access live systems
Principle 4: the investigation lead must perform the acquisition
Principle 2: the person accessing original data must be competent and able to explain the relevance and implications of their actions
blocks.explain: Principle 2 covers the case where accessing original data is necessary. Principle 1 is the default, not a ban; Principle 3 requires an audit trail; Principle 4 puts overall responsibility on the person in charge.

lessons.title: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves

blocks.md:
**Anti-forensics** is any action meant to destroy, hide or falsify evidence. This lesson is written for the investigator: what each family of actions leaves behind and how a defender detects it. It deliberately contains no instructions for doing any of it.

The families, with their MITRE ATT&CK entries:

- **Deleting files** (T1070.004, File Deletion): the content and metadata traces of lessons 3 to 9 remain until overwritten, and the USN journal logs FILE_DELETE.
- **Wiping**: SP 800-86 describes wiping utilities that overwrite media or files with random or constant values. They work well against recovery of the wiped content, but the tool itself leaves execution traces (Prefetch, Amcache, process events) and the overwrite is itself recorded in the change journal (DATA_OVERWRITE).
- **Timestomping** (T1070.006): lesson 5's SI versus FN checks, BASIC_INFO_CHANGE records.

- **Clearing event logs** (now T1685.005, Clear Windows Event Logs): the prereq's event 1102 (audit log cleared) and a hole in the timeline.
- **Hiding data in NTFS attributes** (T1564.004): NTFS files can carry named *alternate data streams* (ADS) besides their main content (SP 800-86 gives `file.txt:Stream1` as the form). Forensic tools list all streams of each MFT record, so ADS are a standard check.
- **Slack and free space**: CyBOK notes that once you know data can be hidden in slack, it is relatively easy to examine, and doing so is a standard step.
- **Destroying recovery data** (T1490, Inhibit System Recovery): deleting Volume Shadow Copies, Windows' point-in-time volume snapshots, which otherwise give investigators older versions of files. ATT&CK lists many ransomware families that do this, and the built-in Windows tools involved, which is what defenders write detections against.
- **Deleting the USN journal**: possible for administrators; Microsoft notes it resets every file's USN to zero, an anomaly in itself.

blocks.title: Every cleanup action leaves a different trace

nodes.label:
USN FILE_DELETE,
free records, bin files

Process events with
telling command lines

scenes.caption: Five cleanup actions an intruder might take after a theft.
File deletion: USN FILE_DELETE records, free MFT records, Recycle Bin `$I` files, carvable content (on disks without TRIM).
Timestomping: SI versus FN mismatch, BASIC_INFO_CHANGE in the journal, the tool's own execution traces.
Clearing the Security log writes event 1102 and leaves a hole in the timeline. The SIEM copy, if logs were forwarded, is untouched.
Deleting shadow copies or the USN journal needs administrator rights and leaves process creation events with telling command lines. Detect those in real time.

blocks.md: **Detect it while it happens.** Destruction of recovery data is a strong signal for a SOC, because ordinary users rarely do it. The prereq chain taught Sigma (a generic rule format that converts to many SIEM query languages). The rule below fires on process creation events for shadow copy deletion through `vssadmin` or `wmic` (both named in ATT&CK T1490) or USN journal deletion through `fsutil` (whose `usn deletejournal` subcommand Microsoft documents).

blocks.code:
title: Recovery and journal evidence being destroyed
status: experimental
description: Shadow copy deletion (ATT&CK T1490) or USN change journal deletion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    shadows_vssadmin:
        Image|endswith: '\vssadmin.exe'
        CommandLine|contains|all: ['delete', 'shadows']
    shadows_wmic:
        Image|endswith: '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains|all: ['shadowcopy', 'delete']
    usn_journal:
        Image|endswith: '\fsutil.exe'
        CommandLine|contains|all: ['usn', 'deletejournal']
    condition: 1 of shadows_* or usn_journal
level: high
blocks.caption: A Sigma rule (parses with pySigma, the reference Sigma library). Tune it for backup software that deletes shadow copies legitimately. It covers three tools only: T1490 also lists diskshadow.exe, wbadmin.exe and bcdedit.exe, each needing its own selection.

blocks.md: The cleanup is evidence too. A 1102 event, a reset journal or deleted shadow copies at 14:35 tell you someone with administrator rights was covering tracks then, which often dates the intrusion better than anything they deleted.

blocks.prompt: An intruder cleared the Security event log on a server. Logs were forwarded to a SIEM every minute. What do you still have?
blocks.reveal:
Nearly everything up to the clearing: the forwarded copies in the SIEM, which the intruder did not touch. On the server itself you also get event 1102 (who cleared it and when) in the fresh log, and the other channels (System, Sysmon, PowerShell) unless they were cleared too, each leaving its own trace.

This is why log forwarding is a preparation item in the prereq: it turns log clearing from destruction into an alert.

blocks.question: Which observation is the strongest sign of deliberate anti-forensics rather than normal use?
options: Files in the Recycle Bin
Last-access times that are hours old
A Security log containing event 1102 shortly after an unusual administrator logon
Large free space on the disk
blocks.explain: Event 1102 records that the audit log was cleared, which ordinary users do not do, and timing next to an unusual admin logon raises it further. Recycle Bin items, lazy access times and free space are normal.

blocks.question: Why does wiping a file often fail to hide that something was wiped?
options: Wiping tools are blocked by NTFS
The wipe overwrites the content but leaves traces such as the tool's execution artefacts and change journal records of the overwrite
Wiped data can always be recovered by carving
Windows keeps a copy of every wiped file in SRUM
blocks.explain: SP 800-86 notes wiping is effective at preventing collection of the content itself, so carving does not undo it. But running a tool and rewriting a file leave execution and journal traces. SRUM stores usage statistics, not files.

lessons.title: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation

blocks.md:
The post gave no exploit details. Under the heading "The completely unrelated", it added that future versions of Signal would periodically fetch files that are never used inside the app, for a small share of long-active installs, because "they look nice, and aesthetics are important in software."

**The response.** A week later Cellebrite told customers it had released UFED 7.44.0.205 and Physical Analyzer 7.44.2 to address a recently identified security vulnerability, and that the Advanced Logical iOS extraction flow was now available in UFED only ([9to5Mac](https://9to5mac.com/2021/04/27/cellebrite-physical-analyzer-iphone/)).

**Why examiners should care.** Lesson 7 of the prereq taught you to hash evidence so you can prove it did not change. That protects the *input*. It says nothing about whether the tool's *output*, your report, is what the evidence says. If the analysis machine is compromised, the hashes still match while the report lies.

blocks.title: How a crafted file could reach an examiner's report (per Signal)

scenes.caption: The phone contains an app file the suspect, or anyone who sent them data, controls.
The analysis suite parses every file, including media, with libraries that were years out of date.
A crafted file makes the parser run code on the analysis machine, which can alter reports without changing hashes or timestamps.
Defences: analyse on an isolated, rebuilt workstation; patch tools; cross-check key findings with a second tool and against the raw extraction.

blocks.code:
import struct, sys
from dissect.ntfs import NTFS                  # tool B: Fox-IT's NTFS parser
img = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
bps, spc = struct.unpack_from('<HB', img, 11)
mft = struct.unpack_from('<Q', img, 48)[0] * bps * spc

def si_created_ours(n):                        # tool A: our own minimal parser
    r = bytearray(img[mft + n*1024 : mft + (n+1)*1024])
    if r[:4] != b'FILE': return None
    uo, un = struct.unpack_from('<HH', r, 4)
    for k in range(1, un): r[k*512-2:k*512] = r[uo+2*k:uo+2*k+2]
    a = struct.unpack_from('<H', r, 20)[0]
    if struct.unpack_from('<I', r, a)[0] != 0x10: return None
    return struct.unpack_from('<Q', r, a + struct.unpack_from('<H', r, a+20)[0])[0]

fs = NTFS(open(sys.argv[1], 'rb'))
same = differ = missing = 0
for rec in fs.mft.segments():
    ours = si_created_ours(rec.segment)
    attr = rec.attributes[0x10]
    if not attr: continue
    if ours is None: missing += 1; continue      # tool A could not read it
    theirs = attr[0].creation_time_ns // 100 + 116444736000000000
    if ours == theirs: same += 1
    else: differ += 1; print('DIFFER at record', rec.segment)
print(f'{same} agree, {differ} differ, {missing} unreadable by tool A')
blocks.caption: cross_check.py: dual-tool verification. Our own minimal MFT parser (tool A) and Fox-IT's dissect.ntfs library (tool B) decode every SI creation time in the test image, and the script also counts records tool A could not read.

blocks.code:
$ python cross_check.py ntfs.bin
932 agree, 0 differ, 1364 unreadable by tool A
blocks.caption: Real output. The parsers agree on all 932 records both could read, but tool A missed 1,364 of the 2,296: it assumes the MFT is one contiguous run, and this image's $MFT is in three fragments. Counting what a tool skipped is part of validation.

blocks.md: A matching hash proves the evidence did not change. It does not prove your tool read it correctly or that your report is untampered. Validation and independent cross-checks cover that gap.

blocks.question: An examiner hashes a phone extraction before and after analysis and the hashes match. Why could the report still be wrong, per Signal's 2021 findings?
options: Code running on the analysis machine could alter reports without changing the extraction's hash
Hashes of phone extractions are unreliable
Matching hashes mean the extraction was empty
The phone may have changed after extraction
blocks.explain: The hash covers the evidence input. Signal described malicious files that could alter Cellebrite reports with no detectable timestamp changes or checksum failures, i.e. the output, not the input.

blocks.question: Which practice most directly addresses the risk that one tool misparses a crucial artefact?
options: Running the same tool twice
Using a newer computer
Hashing the report
Confirming the finding with an independent tool and against the raw data
blocks.explain: A second, independent implementation is unlikely to share the first tool's bug, and checking the raw bytes removes tool interpretation. Running the same tool repeats the same error; hashing the report only shows it did not change later.

lessons.title: Evidence law and writing the expert report

blocks.md:
Everything so far ends in a document that someone else must trust. NIST SP 800-86's reporting phase lists the factors ([SP 800-86](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-86.pdf)):

- **Alternative explanations.** When an event has two or more plausible explanations, each deserves consideration; analysts should methodically try to prove or disprove each one.
- **Audience.** Law enforcement, system administrators and senior management need different levels of detail.
- **Actionable information.** New leads, and things that prevent future harm.

The report should also say what was done, and how tools and procedures were chosen.

**United States.** The Supreme Court's *Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals* (1993), with *General Electric Co. v. Joiner* (1997) and *Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael* (1999), made trial judges gatekeepers of expert testimony, replacing the 1923 *Frye* test. CyBOK summarises the four Daubert criteria ([CyBOK](https://www.cybok.org/media/downloads/Forensics_v1.0.1.pdf)): the method yields testable, falsifiable predictions; it is preferably published in peer-reviewed literature; it has a known error rate; and it is generally accepted in the relevant community.

Federal Rule of Evidence 702, as amended in 2023, lets an expert testify only if the proponent shows it is *more likely than not* that the knowledge will help the court, rests on sufficient facts or data, comes from reliable principles and methods, and reflects a reliable application of them to the case; the committee note adds that each opinion must stay within what that application supports ([FRE 702](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre/rule_702)). Rule 902(14), added in 2017, makes data copied from a device self-authenticating when certified as verified by a process of digital identification, in practice a hash ([FRE 902](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre/rule_902)).

**England and Wales.** The ACPO Good Practice Guide for Digital Evidence ([v5](https://www.digital-detective.net/digital-forensics-documents/ACPO_Good_Practice_Guide_for_Digital_Evidence_v5.pdf)) sets four principles: (1) no action should change data that may later be relied on in court; (2) a person who must access original data must be competent and able to explain the relevance and implications of their actions; (3) an audit trail of all processes applied must be kept, such that an independent third party can repeat them and get the same result; (4) the person in charge of the investigation is responsible for adherence to the law and these principles.

The Forensic Science Regulator Act 2021 made the Regulator's code statutory, in force from 2 October 2023 ([v1](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/statutory-code-of-practice-for-forensic-science-activities)), version 2 from 2 October 2025 ([v2](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/forensic-science-activities-statutory-code-of-practice-version-2)). CyBOK notes the Law Commission proposed criteria building on Daubert.

blocks.title: From bytes to an opinion a court can test

scenes.caption: Evidence received: what it is, its hash at acquisition, its custody. This is the foundation every later statement stands on.
Examination produces facts: "record 41's SI creation time reads 2019-03-01 09:00:00.0000000". Facts state what the data says, with the tool and version used.
Analysis turns facts into inferences: "the SI time was probably rewritten after May 2022". Each inference names the facts it rests on.
Alternative explanations are tested before any opinion: an installer restoring times? an archive extraction? Each is supported or ruled out, in writing.
The opinion states its limits: what is supported, how strongly, and what the evidence cannot show (who sat at the keyboard).

blocks.md:
**A report skeleton that survives cross-examination.**

1. Instructions and the questions you were asked.
2. Evidence received: description, identifiers, hashes, custody.
3. Methods: procedures, tools and versions, validation of those tools.
4. Findings of fact, each traceable to an exhibit and a location (offset, record number, path).
5. Analysis and opinion, with the alternatives considered and why they were rejected.
6. Limitations: what was not examined, gaps such as a trimmed journal or a TRIM-enabled SSD.
7. Appendices: timelines, tool output, glossary for non-specialists.

Write so that ACPO Principle 3 holds: another examiner should be able to repeat every step from your notes and get the same result.

Artefacts identify accounts, devices and volumes, not people. The BTK disk said "Dennis" and a church; identity came from DNA. Write "the account dennis" or "a user of this profile", unless other evidence puts a person at the keyboard.

**Practise legally.** Examine only devices and images you own or are authorised to examine.

- Public disk images: [Digital Corpora](https://digitalcorpora.org/) and NIST's [CFReDS](https://cfreds.nist.gov/) publish training images and reference data.
- Open-source tools: [The Sleuth Kit and Autopsy](https://www.sleuthkit.org/), [PhotoRec](https://www.cgsecurity.org/wiki/PhotoRec), [Eric Zimmerman's tools](https://ericzimmerman.github.io/) for Windows artefacts, and the parsers used in this course.
- Challenge platforms: [CyberDefenders](https://cyberdefenders.org/) and [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) have disk and endpoint forensics labs; [TryHackMe](https://tryhackme.com/) has guided DFIR rooms.
- Rebuild this course's lab: make a small FAT image with a script, delete a file, and recover it three ways (directory entry, carving, and a second tool), then write a one-page report on it.

blocks.question: Under the Daubert criteria as CyBOK summarises them, which question about a new carving tool matters most to admissibility?
options: Is it the most popular tool in the lab?
Was it written in a memory-safe language?
Has its method been tested, with a known error rate, ideally published and generally accepted?
Does it run on Windows?
blocks.explain: Daubert asks for testability, peer review, a known error rate and general acceptance. Popularity, language and platform are not criteria, though popularity can feed general acceptance.

blocks.question: Your analysis shows a USB stick with VSN 1234-ABCD was mounted and a document on it was opened from the profile of user jsmith. Which sentence belongs in the opinion section?
options: J. Smith stole the payroll file
The jsmith profile opened payroll_export.csv from a removable volume with serial 1234-ABCD; this is consistent with, but does not by itself establish, J. Smith personally doing so
The USB stick belongs to J. Smith
No conclusions can be drawn from artefacts
blocks.explain: The opinion should state what the artefacts support (an account and a volume) and its limits. Attributing the act to a person or ownership of the stick needs other evidence; saying nothing ignores real findings.
